case_info.scenario: A 50-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receiving hemodialysis was admitted to the hospital for treatment of calciphylaxis and foot cellulitis. His home medications included sevelamer and hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) every 8 hours as needed, which was increased to every 4 hours as needed in the hospital. Hydromorphone (0.5 mg intravenously as needed) was added for breakthrough pain. He was prescribed chewable lanthanum tablets (500 mg 3 times daily) for treatment of a blood phosphate level of 8.1 mg/dL (reference, 2.5-4.5 mg/dL). On hospital day 7, the patient developed intermittent apneic episodes, during which his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air; heart rate, 86/min; and blood pressure, 106/45 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi and responsiveness to verbal commands only with deep painful stimulus. A chest radiograph showed 4 radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities in the stomach (Figure). After administration of oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula and a naloxone infusion, his oxygen saturation increased to 98% and his mental status improved. The patient reported no foreign body ingestion.
case_info.caption: Chest radiograph showing 4 rounded objects in patient’s stomach.
case_info.explanation: Accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets may cause radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities on imaging studies. Activated charcoal (choice A) and gastric lavage (choice C) are not needed because the patient did not ingest a known toxin. Endoscopy (choice B) is not warranted because the patient had no signs or symptoms of esophageal or gastric outlet obstruction and had no sharp-pointed objects in his esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Foreign body ingestion includes ingestion of true foreign objects and food bolus impaction. Approximately 100 000 cases of upper gastrointestinal tract foreign body ingestion are reported annually in the US, with 80% occurring in children, most commonly between the ages of 6 months and 3 years.1-3Foreign body ingestion in adults is typically due to food bolus impaction and is often associated with esophageal dysmotility, edentulism, and developmental delay.1,2Accidental foreign body ingestion can occur in adults with intoxication or cognitive impairment.2Intentional foreign body ingestion typically occurs in adults with psychiatric disorders, incarcerated individuals seeking release to a medical facility, and those who swallow packets of illicit drugs (“body packing”).1 Most patients with foreign body ingestion are asymptomatic, and most ingested foreign objects pass through the gastrointestinal tract without clinical consequences within 4 to 6 days after reaching the stomach. However, gastrointestinal tract obstruction, perforation, infection, hemorrhage, fistula, or foreign body migration through the digestive wall occur in 1% to 5% of patients with foreign body ingestion.2,4,5These complications often involve areas of gastrointestinal tract narrowing or angulation and are more common in patients with esophageal disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis or in those with esophageal stenosis, webs, or diverticula or previous gastrointestinal surgery or congenital gut malformations.1,5The diagnosis of foreign body ingestion is made with plain radiography to assess the size, location, configuration, and number of ingested radio-opaque objects. Computed tomography imaging is recommended for all patients with foreign body ingestion who have suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation or other complications that may require surgery.2,5 The most common causes of imaging-identified coin-shaped objects in the gastrointestinal tract are coins, batteries, magnets, and certain medications such as barium, lanthanum, and potassium chloride tablets.4,6,7The most common radiopaque ingested foreign bodies are metal objects, such as coins, screws, pins, magnets, button-shaped batteries, and nails.2Lanthanum, a rare earth metal closely related to barium, is a radiopaque phosphate binder that is excreted through the gastrointestinal tract and can be administered as a chewable tablet or as an oral powder. Lanthanum is frequently prescribed for patients with chronic kidney failure and severe hyperphosphatemia and has been reported to cause opacities throughout the gastrointestinal tract on imaging studies.7Common adverse effects of lanthanum include nausea, vomiting, ileus, and diarrhea.7,8 The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends emergent therapeutic esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) within 2 to 6 hours of presentation for foreign bodies that cause complete esophageal obstruction or for sharp-pointed objects or batteries located in the esophagus. Urgent EGD, performed within 24 hours, is recommended for nonobstructing foreign bodies in the esophagus; for sharp-pointed foreign bodies, batteries, and objects longer than 6 cm in the stomach or duodenum; and for magnets within endoscopic reach.1,9Nonurgent EGD, performed within 72 hours, is recommended for blunt objects in the stomach that are larger than 2.5 cm in diameter. Patients with symptomatic ingestion of blunt small objects (other than batteries and magnets) should observed without EGD.1,5,9 Foreign body ingestion associated with hemodynamic instability, severe sepsis, and noncontained extravasation of contrast material requires immediate surgical treatment. Surgery may also be recommended if EGD cannot be performed or if endoscopy fails to extract an ingested foreign body.2,5 Because the patient’s increased opioid dosing frequency caused apneic episodes that led to accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets, hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) was decreased to every 8 hours as needed and intravenous hydromorphone was stopped. Although ultimately not necessary, an abdominal computed tomography scan performed on the same day as the chest radiograph demonstrated dissolving round objects, consistent with ingestion of unchewed lanthanum tablets. The patient did not develop nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, so lanthanum was continued during his hospitalization with clear instructions that these tablets should be chewed prior to swallowing them. At hospital discharge, his phosphate level was normal (3.3 mg/dL). Lanthanum was discontinued, and he continued sevelamer and his home opiate regimen.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

His home medications included sevelamer and hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) every 8 hours as needed, which was increased to every 4 hours as needed in the hospital. On hospital day 7, the patient developed intermittent apneic episodes, during which his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air; heart rate, 86/min; and blood pressure, 106/45 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi and responsiveness to verbal commands only with deep painful stimulus. A chest radiograph showed 4 radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities in the stomach (Figure). case_info.caption: Chest radiograph showing 4 rounded objects in patient’s stomach.
case_info.explanation: Accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets may cause radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities on imaging studies. Activated charcoal (choice A) and gastric lavage (choice C) are not needed because the patient did not ingest a known toxin. Endoscopy (choice B) is not warranted because the patient had no signs or symptoms of esophageal or gastric outlet obstruction and had no sharp-pointed objects in his esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Foreign body ingestion includes ingestion of true foreign objects and food bolus impaction. Approximately 100 000 cases of upper gastrointestinal tract foreign body ingestion are reported annually in the US, with 80% occurring in children, most commonly between the ages of 6 months and 3 years.1-3Foreign body ingestion in adults is typically due to food bolus impaction and is often associated with esophageal dysmotility, edentulism, and developmental delay.1,2Accidental foreign body ingestion can occur in adults with intoxication or cognitive impairment.2Intentional foreign body ingestion typically occurs in adults with psychiatric disorders, incarcerated individuals seeking release to a medical facility, and those who swallow packets of illicit drugs (“body packing”).1 Most patients with foreign body ingestion are asymptomatic, and most ingested foreign objects pass through the gastrointestinal tract without clinical consequences within 4 to 6 days after reaching the stomach. However, gastrointestinal tract obstruction, perforation, infection, hemorrhage, fistula, or foreign body migration through the digestive wall occur in 1% to 5% of patients with foreign body ingestion.2,4,5These complications often involve areas of gastrointestinal tract narrowing or angulation and are more common in patients with esophageal disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis or in those with esophageal stenosis, webs, or diverticula or previous gastrointestinal surgery or congenital gut malformations.1,5The diagnosis of foreign body ingestion is made with plain radiography to assess the size, location, configuration, and number of ingested radio-opaque objects. Computed tomography imaging is recommended for all patients with foreign body ingestion who have suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation or other complications that may require surgery.2,5 The most common causes of imaging-identified coin-shaped objects in the gastrointestinal tract are coins, batteries, magnets, and certain medications such as barium, lanthanum, and potassium chloride tablets.4,6,7The most common radiopaque ingested foreign bodies are metal objects, such as coins, screws, pins, magnets, button-shaped batteries, and nails.2Lanthanum, a rare earth metal closely related to barium, is a radiopaque phosphate binder that is excreted through the gastrointestinal tract and can be administered as a chewable tablet or as an oral powder. Lanthanum is frequently prescribed for patients with chronic kidney failure and severe hyperphosphatemia and has been reported to cause opacities throughout the gastrointestinal tract on imaging studies.7Common adverse effects of lanthanum include nausea, vomiting, ileus, and diarrhea.7,8 The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends emergent therapeutic esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) within 2 to 6 hours of presentation for foreign bodies that cause complete esophageal obstruction or for sharp-pointed objects or batteries located in the esophagus. Urgent EGD, performed within 24 hours, is recommended for nonobstructing foreign bodies in the esophagus; for sharp-pointed foreign bodies, batteries, and objects longer than 6 cm in the stomach or duodenum; and for magnets within endoscopic reach.1,9Nonurgent EGD, performed within 72 hours, is recommended for blunt objects in the stomach that are larger than 2.5 cm in diameter. Patients with symptomatic ingestion of blunt small objects (other than batteries and magnets) should observed without EGD.1,5,9 Foreign body ingestion associated with hemodynamic instability, severe sepsis, and noncontained extravasation of contrast material requires immediate surgical treatment. Surgery may also be recommended if EGD cannot be performed or if endoscopy fails to extract an ingested foreign body.2,5 Because the patient’s increased opioid dosing frequency caused apneic episodes that led to accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets, hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) was decreased to every 8 hours as needed and intravenous hydromorphone was stopped. Although ultimately not necessary, an abdominal computed tomography scan performed on the same day as the chest radiograph demonstrated dissolving round objects, consistent with ingestion of unchewed lanthanum tablets. The patient did not develop nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, so lanthanum was continued during his hospitalization with clear instructions that these tablets should be chewed prior to swallowing them. At hospital discharge, his phosphate level was normal (3.3 mg/dL). Lanthanum was discontinued, and he continued sevelamer and his home opiate regimen.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

4. Frustration

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

His home medications included sevelamer and hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) every 8 hours as needed, which was increased to every 4 hours as needed in the hospital. On hospital day 7, the patient developed intermittent apneic episodes, during which his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air; heart rate, 86/min; and blood pressure, 106/45 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi and responsiveness to verbal commands only with deep painful stimulus. A chest radiograph showed 4 radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities in the stomach (Figure). The patient reported no foreign body ingestion.
case_info.caption: Chest radiograph showing 4 rounded objects in patient’s stomach.
case_info.explanation: Accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets may cause radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities on imaging studies. Activated charcoal (choice A) and gastric lavage (choice C) are not needed because the patient did not ingest a known toxin. Endoscopy (choice B) is not warranted because the patient had no signs or symptoms of esophageal or gastric outlet obstruction and had no sharp-pointed objects in his esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Foreign body ingestion includes ingestion of true foreign objects and food bolus impaction. Approximately 100 000 cases of upper gastrointestinal tract foreign body ingestion are reported annually in the US, with 80% occurring in children, most commonly between the ages of 6 months and 3 years.1-3Foreign body ingestion in adults is typically due to food bolus impaction and is often associated with esophageal dysmotility, edentulism, and developmental delay.1,2Accidental foreign body ingestion can occur in adults with intoxication or cognitive impairment.2Intentional foreign body ingestion typically occurs in adults with psychiatric disorders, incarcerated individuals seeking release to a medical facility, and those who swallow packets of illicit drugs (“body packing”).1 Most patients with foreign body ingestion are asymptomatic, and most ingested foreign objects pass through the gastrointestinal tract without clinical consequences within 4 to 6 days after reaching the stomach. However, gastrointestinal tract obstruction, perforation, infection, hemorrhage, fistula, or foreign body migration through the digestive wall occur in 1% to 5% of patients with foreign body ingestion.2,4,5These complications often involve areas of gastrointestinal tract narrowing or angulation and are more common in patients with esophageal disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis or in those with esophageal stenosis, webs, or diverticula or previous gastrointestinal surgery or congenital gut malformations.1,5The diagnosis of foreign body ingestion is made with plain radiography to assess the size, location, configuration, and number of ingested radio-opaque objects. Computed tomography imaging is recommended for all patients with foreign body ingestion who have suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation or other complications that may require surgery.2,5 The most common causes of imaging-identified coin-shaped objects in the gastrointestinal tract are coins, batteries, magnets, and certain medications such as barium, lanthanum, and potassium chloride tablets.4,6,7The most common radiopaque ingested foreign bodies are metal objects, such as coins, screws, pins, magnets, button-shaped batteries, and nails.2Lanthanum, a rare earth metal closely related to barium, is a radiopaque phosphate binder that is excreted through the gastrointestinal tract and can be administered as a chewable tablet or as an oral powder. Lanthanum is frequently prescribed for patients with chronic kidney failure and severe hyperphosphatemia and has been reported to cause opacities throughout the gastrointestinal tract on imaging studies.7Common adverse effects of lanthanum include nausea, vomiting, ileus, and diarrhea.7,8 The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends emergent therapeutic esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) within 2 to 6 hours of presentation for foreign bodies that cause complete esophageal obstruction or for sharp-pointed objects or batteries located in the esophagus. Urgent EGD, performed within 24 hours, is recommended for nonobstructing foreign bodies in the esophagus; for sharp-pointed foreign bodies, batteries, and objects longer than 6 cm in the stomach or duodenum; and for magnets within endoscopic reach.1,9Nonurgent EGD, performed within 72 hours, is recommended for blunt objects in the stomach that are larger than 2.5 cm in diameter. Patients with symptomatic ingestion of blunt small objects (other than batteries and magnets) should observed without EGD.1,5,9 Foreign body ingestion associated with hemodynamic instability, severe sepsis, and noncontained extravasation of contrast material requires immediate surgical treatment. Surgery may also be recommended if EGD cannot be performed or if endoscopy fails to extract an ingested foreign body.2,5 Because the patient’s increased opioid dosing frequency caused apneic episodes that led to accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets, hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) was decreased to every 8 hours as needed and intravenous hydromorphone was stopped. Although ultimately not necessary, an abdominal computed tomography scan performed on the same day as the chest radiograph demonstrated dissolving round objects, consistent with ingestion of unchewed lanthanum tablets. The patient did not develop nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, so lanthanum was continued during his hospitalization with clear instructions that these tablets should be chewed prior to swallowing them. At hospital discharge, his phosphate level was normal (3.3 mg/dL). Lanthanum was discontinued, and he continued sevelamer and his home opiate regimen.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND, REVISE
You MUST pick a stage from this list.

case_info.explanation: Accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets may cause radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities on imaging studies. Activated charcoal (choice A) and gastric lavage (choice C) are not needed because the patient did not ingest a known toxin. Endoscopy (choice B) is not warranted because the patient had no signs or symptoms of esophageal or gastric outlet obstruction and had no sharp-pointed objects in his esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Foreign body ingestion includes ingestion of true foreign objects and food bolus impaction. Approximately 100 000 cases of upper gastrointestinal tract foreign body ingestion are reported annually in the US, with 80% occurring in children, most commonly between the ages of 6 months and 3 years.1-3Foreign body ingestion in adults is typically due to food bolus impaction and is often associated with esophageal dysmotility, edentulism, and developmental delay.1,2Accidental foreign body ingestion can occur in adults with intoxication or cognitive impairment.2Intentional foreign body ingestion typically occurs in adults with psychiatric disorders, incarcerated individuals seeking release to a medical facility, and those who swallow packets of illicit drugs (“body packing”).1 Most patients with foreign body ingestion are asymptomatic, and most ingested foreign objects pass through the gastrointestinal tract without clinical consequences within 4 to 6 days after reaching the stomach. However, gastrointestinal tract obstruction, perforation, infection, hemorrhage, fistula, or foreign body migration through the digestive wall occur in 1% to 5% of patients with foreign body ingestion.2,4,5These complications often involve areas of gastrointestinal tract narrowing or angulation and are more common in patients with esophageal disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis or in those with esophageal stenosis, webs, or diverticula or previous gastrointestinal surgery or congenital gut malformations.1,5The diagnosis of foreign body ingestion is made with plain radiography to assess the size, location, configuration, and number of ingested radio-opaque objects. Computed tomography imaging is recommended for all patients with foreign body ingestion who have suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation or other complications that may require surgery.2,5 The most common causes of imaging-identified coin-shaped objects in the gastrointestinal tract are coins, batteries, magnets, and certain medications such as barium, lanthanum, and potassium chloride tablets.4,6,7The most common radiopaque ingested foreign bodies are metal objects, such as coins, screws, pins, magnets, button-shaped batteries, and nails.2Lanthanum, a rare earth metal closely related to barium, is a radiopaque phosphate binder that is excreted through the gastrointestinal tract and can be administered as a chewable tablet or as an oral powder. Lanthanum is frequently prescribed for patients with chronic kidney failure and severe hyperphosphatemia and has been reported to cause opacities throughout the gastrointestinal tract on imaging studies.7Common adverse effects of lanthanum include nausea, vomiting, ileus, and diarrhea.7,8 The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends emergent therapeutic esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) within 2 to 6 hours of presentation for foreign bodies that cause complete esophageal obstruction or for sharp-pointed objects or batteries located in the esophagus. Urgent EGD, performed within 24 hours, is recommended for nonobstructing foreign bodies in the esophagus; for sharp-pointed foreign bodies, batteries, and objects longer than 6 cm in the stomach or duodenum; and for magnets within endoscopic reach.1,9Nonurgent EGD, performed within 72 hours, is recommended for blunt objects in the stomach that are larger than 2.5 cm in diameter. Patients with symptomatic ingestion of blunt small objects (other than batteries and magnets) should observed without EGD.1,5,9 Foreign body ingestion associated with hemodynamic instability, severe sepsis, and noncontained extravasation of contrast material requires immediate surgical treatment. Surgery may also be recommended if EGD cannot be performed or if endoscopy fails to extract an ingested foreign body.2,5 Because the patient’s increased opioid dosing frequency caused apneic episodes that led to accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets, hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) was decreased to every 8 hours as needed and intravenous hydromorphone was stopped. The patient did not develop nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, so lanthanum was continued during his hospitalization with clear instructions that these tablets should be chewed prior to swallowing them. At hospital discharge, his phosphate level was normal (3.3 mg/dL). Lanthanum was discontinued, and he continued sevelamer and his home opiate regimen.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A 50-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receiving hemodialysis was admitted to the hospital for treatment of calciphylaxis and foot cellulitis. His home medications included sevelamer and hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) every 8 hours as needed, which was increased to every 4 hours as needed in the hospital. Hydromorphone (0.5 mg intravenously as needed) was added for breakthrough pain. He was prescribed chewable lanthanum tablets (500 mg 3 times daily) for treatment of a blood phosphate level of 8.1 mg/dL (reference, 2.5-4.5 mg/dL). On hospital day 7, the patient developed intermittent apneic episodes, during which his oxygen saturation was 80% on room air; heart rate, 86/min; and blood pressure, 106/45 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed bilateral rhonchi and responsiveness to verbal commands only with deep painful stimulus. A chest radiograph showed 4 radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities in the stomach (Figure). After administration of oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula and a naloxone infusion, his oxygen saturation increased to 98% and his mental status improved. The patient reported no foreign body ingestion.
case_info.caption: Chest radiograph showing 4 rounded objects in patient’s stomach.
case_info.explanation: Accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets may cause radio-opaque coin-shaped opacities on imaging studies. Activated charcoal (choice A) and gastric lavage (choice C) are not needed because the patient did not ingest a known toxin. Endoscopy (choice B) is not warranted because the patient had no signs or symptoms of esophageal or gastric outlet obstruction and had no sharp-pointed objects in his esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Foreign body ingestion includes ingestion of true foreign objects and food bolus impaction. Approximately 100 000 cases of upper gastrointestinal tract foreign body ingestion are reported annually in the US, with 80% occurring in children, most commonly between the ages of 6 months and 3 years.1-3Foreign body ingestion in adults is typically due to food bolus impaction and is often associated with esophageal dysmotility, edentulism, and developmental delay.1,2Accidental foreign body ingestion can occur in adults with intoxication or cognitive impairment.2Intentional foreign body ingestion typically occurs in adults with psychiatric disorders, incarcerated individuals seeking release to a medical facility, and those who swallow packets of illicit drugs (“body packing”).1 Most patients with foreign body ingestion are asymptomatic, and most ingested foreign objects pass through the gastrointestinal tract without clinical consequences within 4 to 6 days after reaching the stomach. However, gastrointestinal tract obstruction, perforation, infection, hemorrhage, fistula, or foreign body migration through the digestive wall occur in 1% to 5% of patients with foreign body ingestion.2,4,5These complications often involve areas of gastrointestinal tract narrowing or angulation and are more common in patients with esophageal disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis or in those with esophageal stenosis, webs, or diverticula or previous gastrointestinal surgery or congenital gut malformations.1,5The diagnosis of foreign body ingestion is made with plain radiography to assess the size, location, configuration, and number of ingested radio-opaque objects. Computed tomography imaging is recommended for all patients with foreign body ingestion who have suspected gastrointestinal tract perforation or other complications that may require surgery.2,5 The most common causes of imaging-identified coin-shaped objects in the gastrointestinal tract are coins, batteries, magnets, and certain medications such as barium, lanthanum, and potassium chloride tablets.4,6,7The most common radiopaque ingested foreign bodies are metal objects, such as coins, screws, pins, magnets, button-shaped batteries, and nails.2Lanthanum, a rare earth metal closely related to barium, is a radiopaque phosphate binder that is excreted through the gastrointestinal tract and can be administered as a chewable tablet or as an oral powder. Lanthanum is frequently prescribed for patients with chronic kidney failure and severe hyperphosphatemia and has been reported to cause opacities throughout the gastrointestinal tract on imaging studies.7Common adverse effects of lanthanum include nausea, vomiting, ileus, and diarrhea.7,8 The American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy recommends emergent therapeutic esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) within 2 to 6 hours of presentation for foreign bodies that cause complete esophageal obstruction or for sharp-pointed objects or batteries located in the esophagus. Urgent EGD, performed within 24 hours, is recommended for nonobstructing foreign bodies in the esophagus; for sharp-pointed foreign bodies, batteries, and objects longer than 6 cm in the stomach or duodenum; and for magnets within endoscopic reach.1,9Nonurgent EGD, performed within 72 hours, is recommended for blunt objects in the stomach that are larger than 2.5 cm in diameter. Patients with symptomatic ingestion of blunt small objects (other than batteries and magnets) should observed without EGD.1,5,9 Foreign body ingestion associated with hemodynamic instability, severe sepsis, and noncontained extravasation of contrast material requires immediate surgical treatment. Surgery may also be recommended if EGD cannot be performed or if endoscopy fails to extract an ingested foreign body.2,5 Because the patient’s increased opioid dosing frequency caused apneic episodes that led to accidental ingestion of whole lanthanum tablets, hydrocodone-acetaminophen (10 mg/325 mg) was decreased to every 8 hours as needed and intravenous hydromorphone was stopped. Although ultimately not necessary, an abdominal computed tomography scan performed on the same day as the chest radiograph demonstrated dissolving round objects, consistent with ingestion of unchewed lanthanum tablets. The patient did not develop nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, so lanthanum was continued during his hospitalization with clear instructions that these tablets should be chewed prior to swallowing them. At hospital discharge, his phosphate level was normal (3.3 mg/dL). Lanthanum was discontinued, and he continued sevelamer and his home opiate regimen.
